procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 24.12.2018 of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Indore in CRR No. 3 of 2018 and CRLA No.3830 of 2018.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Indore affirmed the Judgment of conviction and sentence passed by the Trial Court and dismissed the Criminal Appeal preferred by the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court set aside the Judgment of conviction and sentence passed by the Trial Court and affirmed by the High Court. The matter is remitted back to the trial court for de novo trial by affording proper opportunity to the appellant to defend himself. The trial court and the District Legal Services Authority, Indore, are directed to provide assistance of a senior counsel to the appellant to contest the trial on his behalf. The Supreme Court found that there was no real opportunity for the appellant to cross-examine the experts because they are government servants and could not have attended the Court at the request of an accused in jail.

directions: The matter is remitted back to the trial court for de novo trial by affording proper opportunity to the appellant to defend himself.
The trial court and the District Legal Services Authority, Indore, are directed to provide assistance of a senior counsel to the appellant to contest the trial on his behalf.

issue.issue_text: Whether appellant was aﬀ orded a fair trial; whether he was deprived of his valuable legal rights.

facts: The appellant was convicted for the rape and murder of a three-month-old girl and was sentenced to death.
The entire trial, from the filing of the charge-sheet to the delivery of the judgment, was completed in an expedited manner within 15 days.
The appellant argued that this hasty trial deprived him of a fair trial and his legal rights.
Specifically, forensic experts were not examined in court, which meant the appellant had no opportunity to cross-examine them regarding the DNA evidence.
law: A fair trial for a criminal offense involves not just the technical observance of legal forms but also the substantive application of its principles to find the truth and prevent a miscarriage of justice.
An accused person must be given a "real opportunity" to defend themselves.
The advocate for the accused must be given "sufficient time" to prepare and conduct the case.
Legal aid provided to an accused must be real and meaningful, not merely a formal compliance.
application: The Court reviewed the trial court's order-sheet and found that the trial was conducted in a "hurried manner."
The Court determined that the 15-day timeframe was insufficient and did not provide the appellant a real opportunity to defend himself.
The failure to examine the forensic experts in court deprived the appellant of the crucial right to cross-examine them.
The Court noted that the trial court, on its own, should have adjourned the case to give the appointed lawyer (Amicus Curiae) sufficient time to prepare.
It concluded that while the trial was expedited, this speed did not further the cause of justice and rendered the legal assistance provided to the appellant meaningless.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant was not afforded a fair trial and was deprived of his valuable legal rights. Therefore, it set aside the conviction and sentence and remitted the matter back to the trial court for a new trial, directing that the appellant be provided with the assistance of a senior counsel.

arguments.issue_text: Whether appellant was aﬀ orded a fair trial; whether he was deprived of his valuable legal rights.
appellant_arguments: The trial was conducted hastily, immediately after appointing an amicus curiae counsel, which did not provide sufficient time for the counsel to prepare the defense.
The legal assistance provided was not real or meaningful as the charges were framed and the trial was conducted within a fortnight.
The trial court failed in its duty to grant sufficient time to the appointed counsel for preparation.
The accused was not given a proper opportunity to produce a defense witness.
It is unclear if the defense counsel was supplied with all necessary materials, such as witness statements, to effectively argue the case.
respondent_arguments: The appellant cannot argue that the trial was unfair at this stage, as no objection regarding the hasty completion of the trial was raised earlier.
The conviction and sentence were not illegal because there was clinching scientific evidence against the appellant, which justifies the lower courts' decisions.

cases.case_name: Anil @ Anthony Arikswamy Joseph Vs. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: No hard and fast rule can be laid down as to the time which must elapse between the appointment of counsel and the beginning of the trial; however, the Court of Session must ensure that the time granted to the counsel is sufficient to prepare for the defence based on the circumstances of each case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court has an affirmative duty to grant sufficient time to a defense counsel to prepare their case, and the court's record must reflect this. A mere formal appointment of counsel without adequate time for preparation does not constitute a real opportunity for the accused to defend themselves, and it is immaterial whether the counsel explicitly requested more time.
obiter: No hard and fast rule can be laid down as to the time which must elapse between the appointment of the counsel and the beginning of the trial; the sufficiency of time must be determined by the court based on the circumstances of each case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The trial was procedurally flawed because it was conducted immediately after appointing an amicus curiae counsel, affording only nominal, if any, time for preparation. This haste resulted in the appellant not being given a real or sufficient opportunity to defend himself, which is a violation of the right to a fair trial. The trial court has an affirmative duty to grant sufficient time to counsel for this purpose, and the failure to do so renders the trial a mere farce and violates the minimum standards of due process of law.
legal_tests_applied: A fair hearing, which is inherent in the concept of due process of law, requires that a trial must be a real one, not a sham, farce, or pretense, and it can be vitiated by an overhasty trial.
The appointment of counsel for an accused requires that sufficient time be given to the advocate to prepare the case; a mere formal compliance is insufficient to fulfill the object of the rule.

The trial court has a duty to grant sufficient time to the appointed counsel for preparation, and the record must show that this duty was complied with; the fact that counsel did not ask for more time is immaterial.
policy_considerations: Failure to accord a fair hearing to either the accused or the prosecution violates even minimum standards of due process of law.

The engagement of counsel under the rules is for the purpose of effectively carrying out the duty cast on courts to see that no one is deprived of life and liberty without a fair and reasonable opportunity being afforded to him to prove his innocence.
A trial should be a search for the truth and not a bout over technicalities, and must be conducted under such rules as will protect the innocent and punish the guilty.
Practices like proceeding to trial immediately after appointing counsel reduce the engagement of counsel to a farce.
